newsitem.title: USA: IIF sees emerging economies' record capital flows.
newsitem.headline: IIF sees emerging economies' record capital flows.

text.p: Total net private capital flows to major emerging market economies are expected to reach a record $225 billion this year, up from $208 billion in 1995, the Institute of International Finance said Thursday.

In a briefing for reporters, the institute said emerging economies are set for the strongest levels of economic growth in a decade, growing 5.5 percent in 1997 from a forecast of 4.9 percent this year and 4.2 percent in 1995.

The financial institution's intelligence group also said mainstream investors, such as pension funds and insurance companies, will continue to increase their allocation to emerging markets as net equity flows grow to $110 billion this year from $100 billion in 1995.
It said net flows from non-bank creditors are expected to rise to a record $50 billion from around $17 billion in 1995.

"Equity flows now account for half of total net private flows to emerging markets, with around 70 percent accounted for by direct investment," Charles Dallara, managing director of the IIF, told reporters.
Dallara said mutual funds are intermediating a growing share of both equity and debt flows, and on balance, despite reverses in markets at some times, are building up their positions.
However, the IIF, in a report discussing emerging market activity, said "strong demand for emerging market assets has driven spreads on bonds down to low levels in some countries."
It added that "it will thus be increasingly important to monitor the market for signs of excess that might foreshadow an eventual correction."

In his briefing for reporters, Dallara unveiled a letter to the International Monetary Fund's Interim Committee in which he said that new approaches to avoiding and resolving crises in emerging markets are needed if flows to these countries are to be sustained.
He said they must be grounded on economic, financial and political realities.
